newsitem.title: TAIWAN: New Taiwan opposition party elects chairman.
newsitem.headline: New Taiwan opposition party elects chairman.

text.p: A new opposition party due to be formally established soon elected on Sunday its chairman and vice chairman at a founding meeting, vowing to seek Taiwan's independence.

The meeting elected Lee Chen-yuan, a ranking member of Taiwan's highest academic institution, the Academia Sinica, as chairman of the Taiwan Independence Party. Lin Shan-tian, a renowned law professor, was choses as vice-chairman, state television reported on Sunday.
The party's preparatory office will hold a founding ceremony later on Sunday to pass the group's constitution.

"In the meeting, (we will) express our opinions toward China's suppression..., attitudes toward the current political situation and viewpoints on entering the United Nations," the preparatory office spokesman Lee Yung-chih said on television.
The party has split from the Democratic Progressive Party (DPP).

The DPP, which was formed in 1986 and became legal only after Taiwan lifted martial law in 1987, openly advocates Taiwanese independence and is the island's second biggest political party after the ruling Nationalist Party.
Many of Taiwan's democratic reforms, including the historic direct presidential elections, were promoted by the party.

However, a deepening rift in the island's pro-independence movement led to a decision by a group of activists to formally establish the Taiwan Independence Party on December 12 this year. The group accused the main opposition party of failing to promote independence actively.

The DPP has softened its stance to say that independence would only be declared through a referendum. This followed recent election results that showed most Taiwanese prefer the status-quo to independence or reunification.
Taiwan, which calls itself the Republic of China, and China have been separated since the end of a civil war in 1949. Both sides say they want reunification, but under different terms.
China has threatened to recover the island by force if Taiwan opts for independence.
Taiwan maintains an official policy of anti-independence, but claims it is an "independent political entity" like the government in Beijing.
